utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries, if I am well-informed. Therefore, if we could hear the testimony of the next witness this morning and use any remaining time for small procedural issues still to be dealt with. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And the next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Next witness, Your Honours, good morning, is Dora Sokola.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Sokola.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Sokola, you'll first be examined by Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus is, not unknown to you, I take it, counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Sokola.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: My name is Dora Sokola, and my date of birth is the 19th of May, 1972.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were born, please.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I was born in Zagreb, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And is that where you grew up as well?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court your native language, please.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was this the language you spoke at home throughout your childhood?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And was Croatian also the language of your education as a child?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When did you come to learn English?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I started learning English when I was four years old and then throughout my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Sokola, you have a natural huge speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I was worried about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- slow down. Don't worry about it. We'll come over it but please keep it in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sokola, could you tell the Court a little bit about your education, please.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I was educated through the end of high school in Croatia, and then I spent a year in the US and then came back to Croatia for a year or so to continue my university studies, after which I moved to Belgium where I completed university.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what was your field of study?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: International affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court about your work history, just maybe briefly, with some date, some years, let's say, please?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Okay. In 1991, I believe, I started working once I returned from the US back to Croatia, I started working for ECMM as an interpreter, the European Community Monitoring Mission as an interpreter. And then once I moved to Belgium in 1994, I -- in November 1994 I started working at the ICTY as a field interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what is a field interpreter, please?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: A field interpreter is a -- I was working for the OTP and we went on missions to talk to -- to witnesses. It was in the very early days to investigate potential crimes. So I was interpreting for the investigators and attorneys at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So since that time, that was 1994 --

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Have you been working at the ICTY and, if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I continued to work as a field interpreter until 1995 or so, and then in 1998 I became a full-time language assistant here. And in 1999, I passed the translation professional translator exam with the CLSS in the ICTY and I became a translator, which I continued to do until 2005 within the OTP. And then in 2005, I was head-hunted to go to the State Court in Bosnia as an analyst where I spent two years and then I came back here as an analyst.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Focussing on your work as a language assistant, has your work also involved transcribing and translating audio recordings?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Turning now to the events of the 18th of February, 2013, could I ask you, please, to tell the Court what task were given by the Prosecution on that day.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I received an e-mail, along with several of my colleagues, I received an e-mail asking for assistance in court to listen to any utterances by Mr. Mladic that might be made without having been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And were you told the reason for that request, for that task?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: The sensitivity and the story that the witness had to tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sokola, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your recollection of the circumstances surrounding Mr. Mladic's outbursts which you recorded on the 18th of February. First, do you recall whether the outburst happened during a break or during a hearing?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: It was during a break between the first and the second session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember where during the break or when during the break the outbursts were made?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: It was before the -- the, Your Honours, Judges, came in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall who was present in the courtroom when the accused exclaimed these words?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I recall that most of the Prosecution team was already there, and the outburst occurred as the Defence team came in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe Mr. Mladic's movements during the utterance of these words to the extent you are able to?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: He was speaking as he came in, into the courtroom, and continued to speak until he sat down, until the Judges came in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How is it that you were able to hear his words?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is fairly loud.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you take down any notes of what you heard?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I took down all that I could hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And in what language did you make those notes, please?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I wrote it in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How soon after the accused made these statements did you note them down?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: At the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I call up the next document, I would like to pose a query to the Chamber. During the testimony of Ms. Karall, I called up the e-mail she had sent on the day of the accused's exclamations with her rendition of the words she heard the accused say. It seemed to me not to be improper because it was my understanding that the memory of the witness was not in question but, rather, the accuracy of the content of what she heard the accused say. However, I detected what I thought was perhaps a bit of discomfort on the part of the Chamber when I did that. So before I do that again, I would like to inquire with the Chamber if I may proceed in the same manner with Ms. Sokola, that is, to call up an information report which was prepared with -- by an investigator right after the exclamations were heard and noted down by her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I consult with my colleagues, does the Defence take any position in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, we had no problem with that, and said so earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, are we talking about 30403, 65 ter, or are we talking about the information report 30270?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The latter, Your Honour. The latter, 30270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, the Chamber has no problem with the way in which you intend to proceed as you suggested, so feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 30270. This is an information report taken by an OTP investigator from Ms. Sokola on the 18th of February, 2013.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sokola, do you see the information report taken by investigator Erin Gallagher on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall giving the information that's in this information report to Investigator Gallagher?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you confirm the accuracy and truthfulness of the information you provided as contained in this information report?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And before I ask you to read the quote that you heard Mr. Mladic say into the record, could I just ask you to explain for us what the -- the three dots that appear between some of the phrases, what -- what that means?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: It means that I did not hear exactly the -- the beginning of the sentence, so rather than guess, I put dot, dot, dot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And can you tell us again before you read whether all of these words were spoken right after each other or whether they were different phrases were spoken over a period of time. You described there was a period of time over which he was speaking.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: They were -- they were spoken over a period of time from the moment that Mr. Mladic came in until the time that the Chamber walked in, into the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you please to read the words you heard the accused exclaim in B/C/S aloud?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Branko, is Selmo alive. Mesa Selimovic's Muslim family. I got them out of Mostar. "All of this is correct and I'm proud of them. What the fuck does a Muslim woman want? Ask her about Cicmo. He was a great fighter, killed at Trnovo. Did he rape her? Or Lieutenant-Colonel Miljkovic, did he rape her? Vlasenica -- chief was --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page -- can we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was a request --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was request to the court usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S. Not yet. No. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... to Vlasenica. Cifo's brother-in-law and his daughter Vesna, they were in Vienna later. They had come from Macedonia and they asked me to get the Macedonians out of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sokola, who translated the -- the English notes that you took back into B/C/S as we see in the information report?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know what paper the accused was waving as you describe in the information report?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders into evidence this information report, 30720, as a public exhibit. The redactions at the beginning are the portion that related to Ms. Karall, her evidence. And the redactions at the end relate to what Mr. Mladic exclaimed as he was being removed from the courtroom which the Prosecution does not seek to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I hear of no objections. I see that there are no objections, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30270 receives number P2533, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2533 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sokola, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may get just a moment to consult my client, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have a short moment. And your client is expected to keep the volume of his voice down so that no one can hear your conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, I can hear you even through my earphones, so, therefore, that's not the volume I expect. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Sokola, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Sokola.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you only a couple of questions and let us try to slow down because both you and I tend to speak fast. The first thing I would like to clarify is your task on that day in the courtroom. You spoke about that partly, but I would like to hear the specifics now. What exactly was your task? Were what were you follow specifically?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I -- I was to follow any, as I said, any utterances made by Mr. Mladic off the record at the time when he was not being recorded, so during the breaks, and to record, myself, write down anything he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At what moment did you enter the courtroom with that assignment?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: During the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you together in -- with Maria Karall, in this courtroom at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The moment when you entered the courtroom during the first break, was that -- was Mr. Mladic present in the courtroom at that time?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic was not present at -- in the courtroom at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until that day, did you ever have a similar assignment?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Similar, yes; the same, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you -- were you present in the courtroom with a similar task at any time before the event in question?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no. I don't recall so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who specifically gave you that assignment?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it ever pointed out to you that the communication between a defendant and his Defence counsels is privileged communication?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I was given a task, and I did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand your answer that this was not pointed out to you, or was it ever pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not pointed out to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So may I conclude, then, that it was your task to follow and note down whatever was being said outside the trial, that is, what was being said between the defendant and his Defence counsel and what -- and does not enter the transcript?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: No. My task was to follow what Mr. Mladic said. Not what the Defence attorneys said. Just what Mr. Mladic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever told to follow only what was being said aloud and make an assessment yourself what -- what aloud is? Or were you supposed to note down whatever you were able to hear?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Whatever I was able to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever told to note down only what Mr. Mladic says in connection with the witness or anything he says to his Defence attorney and that you're able to hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you are including, again and again, that the task was to record what Mr. Mladic said to his Defence attorneys. Whereas the witness has now twice explained that all utterances, not excluding the ones that you are referring to, that all utterances were to be written down. So would you please refrain in your question from more or less twisting the previous answer given by the witness. Perhaps you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be briefer and more direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your task was to note down whatever General Mladic was saying to his Defence counsel, no matter whether it related to the witness that testified on that day?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: It is correct that I was told to record -- to note down and follow everything that Mr. Mladic said, not necessarily to his Defence attorneys, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and understand this better. If Mr. Mladic were to speak about his family or his private affairs to his Defence counsel, was it your task to record that too?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now together take another look at document 30270 from the 65 ter list. I will now ask you, Ms. Sokola, if you can tell me which words of the ones that you noted down Mr. Mladic uttered when -- as he was entering the courtroom and where does the text begin that he uttered from his usual place in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question. You are referring to "usual place." Could you be more precise, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take it step by step, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us, out of all of these words that you wrote down, what were the words that Mr. Mladic uttered as he walked into the courtroom as you explained that during the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I wrote down the -- the words, the sentences as -- in -- in the order that they were happening. So he would have been asking about Mesa Selimovic as he entered. I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When he uttered his first sentence, "Branko, is Selmo alive," did you notice who it was that he specifically addressed this question to?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I can tell you what I assumed, that it was his Defence attorney, Branko Lukic, Mr. Branko Lukic. But I was not looking at Mr. Mladic throughout this time because I was also writing things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mesa Selimovic is the first and last name of a well-known Yugoslav writer?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this Yugoslav writer, Mesa Selimovic, passed away many years before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that you heard that, on that occasion, Mr. Mladic mentioned precisely that name, Mesa Selimovic?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: That is what I heard at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These sentences, "Branko, is Selmo alive? Mesa Selimovic, his Muslim family, I got them out of Mostar," were they uttered in a continuous manner or was there an interruption in terms of time between these sentences?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: There may have been a few seconds between each section of the sentence but they seemed to be a continuous phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your next note says: "All of this is correct." And then you have this digression. He's waving a piece of paper. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether it is a book, a single piece of paper, or several pieces of paper that General Mladic was waving?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: It was not a book. If it had been a book, I believe I would have written "book." But I don't recall if it was a single sheet of paper or several.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence that you wrote down says: "Ask her about Cicmo. He was a great fighter, killed at Trnovo. Did he rape her? Or did Lieutenant-Colonel Miljkovic, did he rape her?" Who was it that Mr. Mladic was addressing as he uttered this sentence?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: The Defence team that that was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then what follows is the next sentence that you wrote down, the part that did you not manage to write down, and then: "... to Vlasenica. Cifo's brother-in-law and his daughter Vesna, they were in Vienna later. They had come from Macedonia, and they asked me to get the Macedonians out of Sarajevo." Would you agree with me that this sentence has no contextual link to the previous text and the previous sentence?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between these sentences, was there an interruption, a pause, or did all this happen in a flow, if you will?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: No, there -- there were pauses between these sentences. And -- at which time also the -- Mr. Lukic and other members of the Defence team, if I recall correctly, spoke to -- to Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want to tell us now that there was some communication that you did not write down, something that Mr. Mladic had uttered to his Defence attorneys except for this just before "to Vlasenica"?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that there was -- this was a conversation and that I did not hear what was being said by other people -- people other than Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why I'm asking you. Was there anything else that Mr. Mladic had uttered to his Defence attorneys and that you did not write that down except for what you marked for us here, "to Vlasenica"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I repeat what I said before. The first question is: Was there anything else that Mr. Mladic had uttered and that did you not write down except for what you marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't believe so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just jump in, Mr. Stojanovic. But you didn't write what other people said to Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear what other people said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you didn't write that. And you were not instructed to write what other people said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, just half a moment, half a minute, Your Honours, please, and it will be very quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until -- up to the moment where Mr. Mladic is seated again, and again I repeat: No conversation which is audible for other persons, so that means whispering, otherwise, have you to wait until the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you often take off your earphones when you start your conversation which results in missing my words. Now, fortunately, your volume was down. But would you please not take them off so that you miss my instructions to you. Let's proceed. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Ms. Sokola. What did General Mladic look like as he entered the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase this very vague question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he red in the face?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall this at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he come across as a person who was upset, agitated?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Not particularly. No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The words that he uttered, did he utter them too loud in a way that was not the usual way in which one communicates with one's Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: I have heard Mr. Mladic utter things in court off the record as well and it's always at a certain volume. So I don't -- it wasn't out of the norm, no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It just seems that the witness perhaps didn't understand the question, so I just wanted to be sure that that's clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep things as simple as we can. Are you familiar with the volume with which Mr. Mladic speaks when he consults with counsel? In court, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have -- yes. I have -- I have watched the proceedings before, yes. So I am familiar through that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you also have been today in court, where Mr. Mladic consulted with counsel. Was that at a similar volume as when he spoke when he -- on the date about which you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was -- it was at much lower volume today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was your -- where were you seated in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was seated with the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you seated at the back row closest to the interpreters' booth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When Mr. Mladic entered the courtroom, where was he? Was he at the opposite side of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he come ever any closer to you than being at the very last row of the courtroom closest to the interpreters' booth to, at this moment as you're seated here, to your left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall conclude with the following question. All of this communication, was it between Mr. Mladic and his Defence attorneys?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And at that point in time, there were no Judges in the courtroom and the witness was not in the courtroom either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one more question for you before I give an opportunity to Ms. Marcus for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the volume of Mr. Mladic's voice such that it was easy for you to hear him, or did you have to make a great effort in trying to hear what he said?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: It was very easy to hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means, if I understand you well, that it was so loud as for you to easily hear what he said from the other side of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I -- there seem to be -- I start to my left. Judge Fluegge may have one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us about the words he uttered. The first word you noted down, was that uttered while Mr. Mladic was standing, walking, or sitting?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: He was -- he was walking, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And he continued while he was sitting? Or seated?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has one or more questions for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you were sitting where you were sitting, were you hiding away or were you sitting in such a way that Mr. Mladic could see you?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: No, I believe Mr. Mladic could see me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you alone in the courtroom, other than the team, the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: No, most of the Prosecution team was already here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They were all there.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Mladic could see them too? They were not hiding.

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just a few, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sokola, was it your impression that the accused was trying to have a private conversation with his attorneys when you heard him exclaim these words?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness is being asked to speculate what Mr. Mladic thought or meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The witness is asked the -- for the impression she gained at the time. Now, when evaluating the evidence, what the probative value of such an expression is is a different matter, but she's not invited to speculate. Could you tell us whether you formed an impression about whether the conversation was meant to be with his counsel only, his attorneys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not form an impression whether he intended to speak only to his counsel. But it was not -- the impression I did get was that it was not meant to be a private conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware of which part of his exclamations would have related to the witness testimony and which might not have?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: From the context, yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you asked to conduct this kind of analysis?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Stojanovic, I do understand that you have one or more questions triggered by either questions of the Bench or questions by Ms. Marcus. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, in response to Judge Orie's question, at one point in time you said that this was loud communication and that you could hear that. This is what I'm asking you now: How is it possible, then, that part of this communication that you described in such a way you did not write down and you could not hear?

utterances.speaker: DORA SOKOLA
utterances.text: There were other people coming into the court -- at all -- it was during the break so other people were coming into the Prosecution side of the court. It may have -- may be that I was distracted for a second and did not hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has one more question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the other people talk at the same volume of voice as Mr. Mladic was speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would be the difference, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic was louder than the rest of the people in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Ms. Sokola, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you for coming to this courtroom and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. You are excused, and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, and I do apologise to my learned friend, I was asked by our client to make it possible for him to be transported even if we are going to stay in court longer because at 11.00 he has a religious service scheduled and he would like to attend. So I'm going to ask you if we continue to deal with procedural matters, we do have Mr. Mladic's consent to go on, but could he please be transported to where he would like to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Mladic waives his right to be present in court, nothing, as far as the Chamber is concerned, opposes him being transported back. The Chamber, however, is not in a position to give any instructions or orders in relation to transportation, but if that could be achieved, I think the Chamber would fully support that so that Mr. Mladic would be back in time to -- to attend that ceremony. Even -- I have a few matters I would like to deal with before the break, mainly asking the Prosecution -- the Defence to consider whether there's any response. If Mr. Mladic would prefer already to leave the courtroom at this moment, it -- he is granted leave to do so. So if Mr. Mladic even before the end of this session would prefer to leave ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note that his waiver is not on the record. I just thought that might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although expressed by counsel. Counsel says that he is and we usually rely on -- I think that's what Mr. Stojanovic said. So I'm asking -- we continue deal with procedural matters. We do have Mr. Mladic's consent to go on, but could he please be transported, which is understood as a waiver of his right not to be present. Is that a proper understanding, Mr. Stojanovic? I see Mr. Mladic nodding yes, which is hereby put on the record as well. And he repeats it. If Mr. Mladic would like to be escorted out of the courtroom at this moment, then security is invited to escort ... no, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, I just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since this is not going to last for a long time, then you can continue with Mr. Mladic's consent. He will stay on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I deal with a few matters only at this moment. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I just wanted to mention that I would like to make a brief bar table submission that came up as a result of the cross-examination, but I can do that at the start of the next session or as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, now Mr. Mladic is aware of your intention, and we'll see whether he intends to remain with us or whether he waives his right to be present. For the first matter I have to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. On the 16th of October, the Prosecution informed the Defence and the Chamber that it had uploaded a missing B/C/S translation for P2198 MFI'd, as well as a revised English translation for P1110, MFI'd. The Defence stated that it would respond that same day. We have not heard from the Defence, however. Can you express the Defence position at this moment for P2198, Mr. Stojanovic? If -- if not, we'd like to hear from you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we shall try to respond immediately after the break. We just need to identify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, finally, a short observation in relation to Rule 65 ter 28036. On the 18th of October, we dealt with this Rule 65 ter number. I think 28036 was initially tendered through Witness RM506 and the Defence then indicated that they needed to consider whether they have any objections to admission. They were instructed to do so not later than that same week, which is found at transcript page 1711. That's -- seems to be a mistake. It could not possibly be. But so my reference to the transcript is inaccurate. Nevertheless, the Chamber would like to hear the Defence's position in relation to 65 ter 28036. Perhaps also after the break, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Our colleague Mr. Ivetic is working on that, and I believe that this response is going to be filed today, or it is already taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would it assist the parties if we take a slightly longer break and deal with a few other procedural matters after the break? Since there's no other witness available, we might take a bit more time. Then I suggest a break until quarter past 11.00. Would that do? I hear of no objections. If Mr. Mladic wants to return to the UNDU, as I said before, the Chamber has no objections. And if Mr. Mladic does not return in the courtroom after the break, this will be understood as an explicit waiver to be present. We take a break and we resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hereby put on the record that Mr. Mladic is not present in court. The Chamber understands his absence as a waiver of his right to attend the proceedings. Perhaps, Ms. Marcus, you announced that you would raise a bar table submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. It's one document. It's 65 ter 30266. This was the demonstrative exhibit that was distributed in the courtroom during the testimony of RM048 and Mr. Stojanovic has informed me that he has no objections to this being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 30266 receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P2534, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should be under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2534 is admitted under seal. Nothing else, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just more thing I wanted to put on the record in relation to this and that would be the end of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I just wanted refer the Chamber to the courtroom video, which was admitted as P2181, at clips 5 and 6, and this is all in relation to the evidence of Ms. Sokola. And to Exhibits P357 at page -- in particular, page 69 in the original B/C/S handwritten version, and P359, pages 17 and 18, pardon me, in the handwritten B/C/S original. The Prosecution's submission is that the document that was just admitted, P2534, and these two exhibits, portions of exhibits which I've just mentioned, are the papers that Mr. Mladic was waving during the time he made the utterances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's argument already, although what he showed or not is interpretation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was just to put it on the record to guide the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, any matter from the Defence to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must admit that I haven't fully understood on what basis the Prosecutor is making this suggestion. Where is this found at in the witness's statement that Mr. Mladic was waving a sheet of paper? It doesn't follow. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- let me try to explain to you how I understood how the Chamber understood it. That, although the witness did not -- said, could not tell us, what exactly it was that Mr. Mladic had shown, that it is, nevertheless, the Prosecution's position that the portions of P357 and P359 mentioned by Ms. Marcus were the documents the -- Mr. Mladic was showing. That is the Prosecution's position in relation to this evidence, even where the witness could not identify it -- could not identify the papers as such. That's how I understood it. Yes. Then, I'll move on. Mr. Stojanovic, even after 65 ter 30270 was already admitted as P2533, you still referred to the -- to the 65 ter number. I hereby put on the record that it was admitted as P2533. Now, I have a few more matters which I'd like to deal with. The -- for the first one, I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. My next issue deals with Exhibits P1501 and P1502. On the 28th of May of this year, the Chamber admitted Exhibits P1501 and P1502 into evidence through Witness RM322. These are 156 and 158 pages long respectively, while, as noted on transcript page 11663, P1502 is the original form of P1501. On the 31st of May, the Chamber noted in court that only a few passages of the notebook were used with Witness RM322 and requested the Prosecution to select the pages on which it wished to rely upon. The Prosecution replied that it intended to use the notebook with other witness -- with another witness as well, including Witness Butler. The Chamber then observed that it would wait and see how the notebook would be used in the future, and you can find this on transcript page 11869. So far, P1501 was used by the Prosecution in court with Witness Salapura and Witness Butler. It was also used by the Defence with Witness RM318. The Chamber now requests the Prosecution to clarify which pages of the notebook it intends to rely upon, to redact P1501 and P1502 accordingly, and upload new versions into e-court. When the Prosecution has done so, it should inform the Chamber and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, we move on unless there's anything you'd like to raise in relation to what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next item is dealing with some conditionally admitted Rule 92 bis materials. Some witnesses' evidence from the Chamber's decision on the 15th, the 17th, and the 22nd Rule 92 bis motion was admitted on the condition that declarations and attestations be provided. The Chamber has reviewed the relevant documentation and hereby confirms admission of P2446, P2451, P2452, P2455, P2465, and P2487. The next matter I would like to deal with is a decision by the Chamber in relation to protective measures for Witnesses RM029 and RM073. On the 6th of February, 2013, the Prosecution filed a motion in relation to Witness RM029 requesting the protective measures of face and voice distortion, pseudonym, and redaction of the witness's name and other potentially identifying information from the witness's statement. On the same date, the Prosecution filed a motion in relation to Witness RM073 requesting the protective measures of pseudonym, and redaction of the witness's name and other potentially identifying information from the witness's statement. In relation to both witnesses, the Prosecution contends that protective measures are necessary as the witnesses are fearful for their safety in the event of their identity becoming known and further submits that the granting of measures would not impact upon the accused's fair trial rights with -- fair trial rights. With regard to Witness RM029, the Prosecution also submits that the witness resides in an area where certain of the crimes described in the witness's statement were committed. On the 20th of February, 2013, the Defence filed a response to each of the above motions, arguing in relation to both that the Prosecution requests are based on generic and vague fears rather than real fears for the safety of the witnesses, and emphasising that the accused is entitled to a public trial. The Chamber refers to the applicable law set out in its "Decision on Prosecution motion for protective measures for Witness RM115," dated the 15th of August, 2012. At the outset, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution has merely relied upon the generic information provided in the investigator's statements annexed to the motions without expanding on how the test for protective measures has been met for either witness. The Chamber notes that Witness RM029's evidence has been admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis and, therefore, the request for protective measures, in so far as it relates to face and voice distortion, is moot. As regards the remainder of the request regarding Witness RM029, the Chamber considers that the witness provides mainly generic information regarding detention conditions, and while he refers to one alleged direct perpetrator in his statement, the witness was informed of his name by other detainees. Accordingly, there was an insufficient basis to conclude that this evidence may antagonize persons residing in the area where the witness lives. With regard to Witness RM073, the Chamber notes that the witness provides evidence regarding incidents which purportedly occurred while in detention and identifies a number of alleged direct perpetrators. However, the Chamber considers that it is unknown whether the alleged direct perpetrators reside in the same area as the witness. There is an insufficient basis to conclude that this evidence may antagonize persons residing in the area where the witness lives. Weighing the reasons provided in the motions against the right of the accused to a public trial, the Chamber considers that there is an insufficient basis to conclude that protective measures are justified for either witness, and, accordingly, denies the Prosecution's -- Prosecution motions. And this concludes the Chamber's decision and, as a result, the Chamber lifts the confidentiality of the exhibits admitted through these two exhibits in its decision of the 23rd of September, 2013. Next, I will deliver a decision on the admission of P1087. On the 1st of March, 2013, the Prosecution tendered into evidence with Witness Erin Gallagher the Srebrenica map book bearing Rule 65 ter number 28747. The Defence objected to the admission of portions of map book on the grounds that the sources of information appearing in some of the maps were not identified and that the exhibit could only be introduced as a demonstrative exhibit through witnesses with personal factual knowledge about its contents. This can be found at transcript pages 9462 to 9463. The Chamber marked the exhibit for identification as P1087. The parties reiterated their submissions on the admission of P1087 during the housekeeping session of the 25th of July, 2013. With respect to the requirements for admissibility into evidence pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Chamber first notes that the exhibit contains maps that the Prosecution submits relate to various VRS zones of responsibility and several alleged crime sites in the Srebrenica area. The Chamber also notes the evidence of Witness Gallagher in this regard. The Chamber finds, therefore, that the exhibit is relevant to Counts 2 through 8 of the indictment and has probative value for the purpose of admission into evidence. The Chamber considers that the Defence submissions on the sources and the purpose of the exhibit are matters that go to the weight the Chamber will ultimately give to the maps in light of all the evidence before it. The Chamber takes this opportunity to emphasise, as it has done in relation to similar map collections which it has admitted into evidence, that it considers the map book mainly as a reference and the Prosecution's markings and descriptions to be primarily illustrations of the Prosecution's case which need to be proven by evidence. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber admits P1087 into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Next item is a corrigendum. A short corrigendum in relation to the Chamber's decision on the 21st Rule 92 bis motion which was filed on the 16th of October, 2013. In the disposition, under (ii), Mihajlo Galic, point (a), transcript pages 10625, column 22, and 10626, column 21, should be separated by a dash and not by a comma. Further, under (iii), Danko Gojkovic, point (c), the decision should read transcript page 2894, line 3, instead of 728 -- 72894, line 3. Yes. I started to misspeak, but then everything is now clear on the record. I move on and deliver the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's request to add eight documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. On the 20th of September, 2013, the Prosecution requested the addition of eight documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. These documents are related to Witness RM507. The Chamber notes that the Defence has not opposed the addition. Having reviewed the documents, the Chamber is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to add them -- to have them added to the exhibit list. The Prosecution is hereby granted leave to add the documents to its exhibit list. I move on to the next item which deals with outstanding issues related to the testimony of Emir Turkusic. I whether address several outstanding issues which arose during the testimony of Emir Turkusic from the 27th to the 30th of August, 2013. With regard to Exhibit P2043, the Prosecution was instructed to check the English translation on pages 19 and following of the document because some words are considered illegible, even though Mr. Lukic was able to read them. This can be found on transcript pages 15936 to 15937. On transcript page 15946, the Defence was instructed to draw a line with a certain angle on Exhibit D351. The Defence is now instructed to upload a new version of D351 containing the mentioned line, and the Registry is already instructed to replace D351 with the new version of D351 as soon as it is available. With regard to D356, MFI'd, the parties were instructed to inform the Chamber if they agree which excerpts of the rule-book and another rule-book for 120-millimetre mortars should be tendered. This can be found on transcript page 15943. Further, concerning D357, MFI'd, a map, the Defence was instructed to provide the Prosecution with transcript references where the witness testifies about the map so as to resume the discussion on admission. This can be found on transcript page -- pages 15943 to 15945. The parties are instructed to comply with all these instructions within seven days and inform the Chamber when they have been done. I move onto my next item which deals with revised translations. I think I dealt with them already before the break, but we were still waiting for the Defence's position in relation to MFI 2198. Mr. Stojanovic, any report on 2198? I should say P2198.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will proceed in the same order. P52918 is a translation from the original French into English, and we were to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- if you wouldn't mind. There seems to be -- there may be a problem. I was talking about 2198, whereas you refer, as it was translated to us, to P52918, which is at least a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe I said P2198. And as far as our Defence is concerned, I kindly request some more time for us to take a position because the original document is in French, which we do not speak. P1110, we got an English translation and have no objection to the admission of this document. And we are still to take a position as regards document 28036. We have no complaint to that save for our general complaint to the admission of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's deal with them separately. P2198, you're asking for more time. How much more time would you need, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The end of this week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It took me more time to learn French, but if you can do it within this week, Mr. Stojanovic, it's highly appreciated. Then, Madam Registrar, for P1110, MFI'd, have you -- has a revised English translation been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been uploaded. You're hereby instructed to replace the newly uploaded English translation -- no, to replace the old English translation by the newly uploaded one. And, once this is done, P1110 is admitted into evidence. Then we move to 65 ter 28036. We do understand the remaining objection ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Madam Registrar, would you please assign -- give us a number for 65 ter 28036.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28036 receives number P2535, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2535 is admitted into evidence. The next item I'd like to deal with is a corrigendum to the Chamber's decision on the 20th Rule 92 bis motion. On the 25th of September, 2013, the Chamber issued its decision on the Prosecution's 20th Rule 92 bis motion. Therein, it instructed the Registry to change the status of evidence admitted through Witness RM027 and RM704 from confidential to public unless the Prosecution would file motions for protective measures for these witnesses. The Prosecution advised the Chamber that Witness RM704 was granted protective measures in a prior case. Accordingly, the Chamber withdraws its instruction to the Registry to lift the status of the witness's admitted evidence. Regarding Witness RM027, the Prosecution advised the Chamber that one associated exhibit, namely, Rule 65 ter 13375, has been placed under seal in the Tadic and the Karadzic cases. The Chamber requests the Prosecution to provide further information within one week why this exhibit should be kept confidential and defers its final decision on this exhibit's status. Until then, the exhibit remains under seal. The last item on my agenda deals with the Chamber's statement on the further scheduling of the case. With all but one evidentiary motion by the Prosecution filed, the Chamber would like to give the parties some impression of its current scheduling expectations. The Prosecution is expected to rest its case in November 2013. The Chamber may need some time to decide on all pending evidentiary motions so as to close the Prosecution's case. The Chamber expects that the Prosecution's case be closed by January 2014. Any Rule 98 bis submissions should be made soon thereafter, and the Defence should be ready to do so towards the end of January or early February. In this respect, the Defence should inform the Chamber as soon as possible whether it, in fact, intends to bring a Rule 98 bis motion. Should there be a need for a Defence case, the Defence should be ready to start its presentation of evidence around February or March 2014. A Scheduling Order with exact dates will follow in due course. This was all the Chamber had on its agenda. Any questions or any further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to inform the Chamber, update the Chamber on two additional outstanding matters. One relates to documents that were going to be tendered from the bar table in relation to Witness Riedlmayer. At page 17886, my colleague Mr. Traldi informed the Chamber that he may have a brief bar table submission depending upon what areas are challenged. Mr. Traldi has, in fact, approximately eight documents, and he is currently in discussion with the Defence to see whether they could reach an agreement on -- on those documents. That's just to put that -- to inform the Chamber. The other aspect -- the other item I wanted to mention to the Chamber relates to Witness Jeremy Bowen. There are some pending documents; namely, his statement and the -- and the excerpts of his prior transcript, which are MFI'd as P2515 and P2516, as well as eight associated exhibits which haven't yet been tendered. So they remain with their 65 ter numbers. The Prosecution would -- will contact the Defence and will try to see if an agreement can be reached, and we will keep the Chamber informed of the update on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for these updates. Nothing to decide at this moment for the Chamber, I see. We'll hear from the parties soon. Any other matter? If not, we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 22nd of October, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of October, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.55 a.m.,
